Scaling correction factor should be caliculated as the equation:
   (Unadjusted chi-square value / The Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square).

If so,  11736.236  /  7654.695 = 1.5332. 
But, this value is not the same as the scaling correction factor described above (1.653).

Would you tell me why there is the difference between the two values?
Would you please tell me how to get "true" scaling correction factor?

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How to calculate scaled correction factor in DWLS estimator?
parts:
Scaling correction factor should be caliculated as the equation:
   (Unadjusted chi-square value / The Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square).

Would you tell me why there is the difference between the two values?

That is only the case with so-called mean-adjusted stats (e.g., using MLM or WLSM).  DWLS estimation is by default accompanied by a more robust mean- and variance-adjusted (or scaled & shifted) stat (i.e., WLSMV; MLMV is another such stat).
Would you please tell me how to get "true" scaling correction factor?

You add the shift parameter.

11736.236 / 1.653 + 552.687

7652.648 # robust chisq, within rounding error; use fitMeasures() for more precision

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How to calculate scaled correction factor in DWLS estimator?
parts: how does lavaan get the chi-square difference, 56.595?

It is a robust correction of the raw difference between the (unadjusted) values in the "Chisq" column.  The standard "anova" class in R does not have a place to store the scale and shift parameters for the robust difference test, but it works the same way.  That has always bothered me... perhaps the scale/shift parameters could be added as attributes, then printed in the header (lavaan NOTE).

Second, although a significant difference of chi-square (p = .002) suggests that the former model (M) is better than the second model (M10), 
other fit indices (cfi.scaled, tli.scaled, and rmsea.scaled) suggests that the second model (M10) is better than the former one (M).  
Considering which model is better, which information should I rely on?

There is no contradiction.  Different measures tell you different things.  The chi-squared difference test is a test of the H0 of exact equality between models.  The fit indices adjust for parsimony and sample size, such that they are less like test statistics and more like measures of effect size.
Third, although I used such fit indices as cfi.scaled, tli.scaled, and rmsea.scaled, are there other indices I should refer to?

It is not clear you should refer to those.  If you disregard a test statistic with known properties (e.g., Type I error rate), then you should have a good theoretical defense for preferring other measures, and for understanding what they tell you.
